brief.interpretation: Read literally: one announcement email to people who have not bought, making the case for why it matters now and what to do next. I am treating "launch" as "this is available and here is the first useful thing to do with it" — not a discount, not a demo push, not an onboarding note to existing users. The audience was chosen for me: the ops/IT generalist standing up an internal Slack answer-bot over company docs. That segment is rated adjacent and review_first, and the field is ahead of us on breadth, quality, speed, control and security — so the email cannot win by being a better assistant than what a workspace already bundles. It wins only by being the exact shape of the job this reader already has open: handbook questions, answered in Slack, over their own documents. brief.promise: You can have an agent answering handbook questions inside Slack, grounded in your own documents, without building or owning the retrieval layer that makes it work.
brief.orientation: For this buyer, orqAgent is a hosted place to configure one agent over their own handbook documents and attach it to Slack, with every answer logged as a run, instead of assembling Slack events, a vector store and a model API themselves.
brief.arc: Single email, so the whole arc happens inside it: from "an internal answer-bot is a build somebody here would have to own" to "it is a configuration over documents I already have, and I can test it against last week's questions before anyone else sees it." The email opens on the reader's recurring problem, names what people do today, states plainly what is now available and how it is put together, and ends on a first test that is small enough to run alone.
brief.sequence_rationale: One email, so the only real decision is which single claim gets the slot. I chose the assembly claim — documents in, answers in Slack, no retrieval layer to stand up — over the two obvious alternatives. Cost and analytics (every answer is a logged run with latency and spend) is the stronger argument later, once the reader is deciding whether to open the bot to the whole company; leading with it answers a question they have not asked yet. Price is out on principle: the competitor read puts $0/$29 squarely in table stakes, five competitors say the same thing, and this company's own pricing tables contradict each other across pages, so any number beyond the free sign-up itself is a trust liability rather than an argument. The maintenance objection gets answered inside the mechanism rather than as a separate section: the vector store is not theirs to run and Slack is an OAuth install, not an events pipeline. Everything about proof is thin and I am not pretending otherwise — there is no customer, no logo, no usage figure anywhere in the material, so the email asserts what the product does and invites a ten-minute test against the reader's own handbook instead of asking them to believe a claim about somebody else. The single thing you could send us that would most change this campaign: which customers or quotes may we name?
